exercises.prompt: Implement initials(first, last) so it returns the two uppercase initials of a first and last name. initials('ada', 'lovelace') returns 'AL'. Assume both names are non-empty.
hints: You need the first character of each name, joined together and forced to uppercase.
Read the first characters with first[0] and last[0]; an f-string f'{first[0]}{last[0]}' drops them side by side.
return f'{first[0]}{last[0]}'.upper() — uppercasing the joined pair handles both letters at once.

exercises.prompt: Implement is_palindrome(s) so it returns True when s reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case, and False otherwise. is_palindrome('Anna') is True and is_palindrome('hello') is False. The empty string counts as a palindrome.
hints: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, so compare the word against its own reverse — ignoring case.
s.lower() normalizes the case, and the slice s[::-1] gives the reversed string.
return s.lower() == s.lower()[::-1]; the empty string reverses to itself, so it counts as a palindrome.

exercises.prompt: Implement truncate(s, max_len) so that when s is longer than max_len characters it is cut to the first max_len characters followed by '...', and otherwise s is returned unchanged. truncate('hello world', 5) returns 'hello...'; truncate('hi', 5) returns 'hi'.
exercises.solution:
def truncate(s, max_len):
    return s if len(s) <= max_len else f'{s[:max_len]}...'
hints: Compare the string's length against max_len first; only the too-long case gets an ellipsis.
len(s) measures the string and s[:max_len] keeps its first max_len characters.
return s if len(s) <= max_len else f'{s[:max_len]}...' builds the shortened form with an f-string.

exercises.prompt: Implement reverse_words(s) so it returns the words of s in reverse order, joined by single spaces. reverse_words('hello world') returns 'world hello'. A single word is returned unchanged, and the empty string returns the empty string. Assume words are separated by single spaces.
hints: Break the sentence into its words, reverse their order, then glue them back with spaces between.
s.split(' ') gives a list of words, the slice [::-1] reverses that list, and ' '.join(...) rebuilds the string.

exercises.prompt: Implement first_word(s) so it returns the portion of s before the first space. If there is no space, return the whole string. first_word('hello world') returns 'hello'; first_word('single') returns 'single'. Assume s has no leading space; the empty string returns the empty string.
hints: Find where the first space sits; the answer is everything before it, or the whole string when there is no space.
s.find(' ') returns the position of the first space, or -1 when there is none — the -1 case means return s unchanged.
Set i = s.find(' '), then return s if i == -1 else s[:i].
